description:
We are a two-person team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, working on the "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map" challenge.

Passionate about AI, robotics, software development, mapping, and space exploration, our goal is to build a creative, technically solid, and useful Mars navigation tool that combines innovation with a fun and memorable team identity
summary: Plan a science Marswalk in Jezero Crater. Mars Pathfinder is a working web prototype that compares routes to team-selected science objectives on real Martian terrain. The Meowrtian combines MRO/HiRISE imagery and stereo elevation data with USGS SIM 3464 geology and documented Mars 2020/Perseverance photographs. Two A* modes compare shortest horizontal distance with a slope-penalized alternative under the same terrain constraints. The English interface exposes data provenance, uncertainty and downloadable results. It supports education and mission concept discussions and does not certify astronaut safety.
details:
The Problem

Planning a scientific Marswalk requires more than choosing the shortest path. Astronauts exploring Mars need to understand terrain elevation, slopes, geological context and uncertainty before selecting a route.

Our Solution

Mars Pathfinder is an interactive web application for exploring a region of Jezero Crater using authentic NASA and USGS data.

We combined MRO/HiRISE orbital imagery and stereo elevation data, USGS geological mapping, and documented Mars 2020/Perseverance photographs. Users can explore terrain layers, examine three team-selected scientific objectives, and plan traverses across the Martian surface.

Our route-planning engine uses the A* search algorithm on a 10-meter terrain grid. It calculates two alternatives:

  • Route A — Shortest: minimizes horizontal travel distance.
  • Route B — Slope-aware: penalizes steep terrain while applying the same traversability constraints.

Both algorithms reject unavailable terrain and slopes exceeding the selected model threshold.

Real Results

Our "Start Mission" feature automatically plans a traverse to science objective M3.

The validated experiment produced:

  • Route A: 3,035.81 m distance, 36.39 m cumulative ascent, 14.54° maximum modeled slope.
  • Route B: 3,118.65 m distance, 31.88 m cumulative ascent, 9.02° maximum modeled slope.

Route B is only 82.84 m longer, while reducing cumulative ascent by 4.51 m and maximum modeled slope by 5.52°.

Users can inspect both routes, compare their elevation profiles, explore relevant geological information and download reproducible results in JSON format.

Technology and Validation

We built the application using Next.js, React, TypeScript, OpenLayers and a deterministic A* routing engine with Web Workers. Python, Rasterio/GDAL and geospatial libraries were used to prepare the scientific datasets.

Validation included 72 passing Vitest tests, 22 Python tests, independent Dijkstra comparisons, type checking, production builds and browser testing.

The live application is hosted on Netlify, and its original source code is publicly available under the Apache-2.0 license:

https://github.com/EduardoManzanoAlcaraz/mars-pathfinder-the-meowrtian

Impact and Limitations

Mars Pathfinder demonstrates how real planetary data can be transformed into an accessible, interactive tool for comparing scientific exploration routes.

Our prototype supports education, scientific communication and early mission-concept planning. It does not provide operational astronaut safety certification. Soil stability, small obstacles, radiation, weather and crew endurance remain outside the current model.

We distinguish official NASA/USGS observations from terrain derivatives, selected objectives and routing assumptions created by our team.
